abstract: Chronic cutaneous wounds are often described as disorders of inflammation, infection, perfusion, or extracellular matrix turnover, yet these categories do not fully explain why a wound that initially detects injury fails to re-enter a coordinated program of repair. This Perspective proposes a unifying model in which the nucleus acts as a damage integrator at the wound edge. Mechanical strain, osmotic swelling, oxidative stress, chromatin fragmentation, and mitochondrial injury converge on nuclear-envelope tension, nuclear rupture, cytoplasmic deoxyribonucleic acid sensing, and senescence-associated transcription. When the signal is brief and spatially restricted, it can support leukocyte recruitment, keratinocyte migration, matrix remodeling, and early host defense. When it is amplified by diabetes, aging, tissue stiffness, biofilm-compatible inflammation, or defective autophagic and efferocytic clearance, the same pathway becomes a self-reinforcing loop that sustains interferon signaling, inflammasome activity, endothelial dysfunction, fibroblast memory, and impaired epidermal differentiation. The review integrates evidence from single-cell wound atlases, mechanobiology, innate immune deoxyribonucleic acid sensing, mitochondrial stress, macrophage biology, senescence, microbiome studies, and smart biomaterials. It argues that future wound therapeutics should not simply accelerate closure, but should classify and reset the temporal polarity of nuclear damage responses. Nucleus-aware dressings, local signal-gated inhibitors, senolytic or senomorphic interfaces, and biomaterials that reduce pathological mechanical memory may provide more precise ways to convert chronic wound fields into regenerative ones.
